questions.prompt: What is the first problem Chapter 3 attacks?
choices: Forecast language that sounds useful but stays too vague to measure
A lack of enough professional credentials among forecasters
An overreliance on historical examples

explanation.gentle: The chapter starts by showing that fuzzy wording blocks real learning because nobody can score it cleanly later.
explanation.direct: Ambiguous forecast language is the first structural weakness the chapter targets.
explanation.competitive: Blur is where bad forecasts first hide.

questions.prompt: Why does Sherman Kent matter in this chapter?
choices: He argued that verbal hedges are more flexible than numbers
He pushed probability language toward numerical ranges
He proved that intelligence work should avoid forecasting

explanation.gentle: Kent matters because he tried to turn slippery forecast language into something explicit enough to check later.
explanation.direct: His contribution is numerical probability language as an accountability tool.
explanation.competitive: He made the forecast hold still long enough to be judged.

Whether a forecaster uses enough technical terms
Whether all predictions stay close to 50 percent

explanation.gentle: Calibration asks whether your confidence levels line up with what actually happens over time.
explanation.direct: It measures alignment between stated certainty and later outcomes.
explanation.competitive: Calibration checks whether your confidence scale tells the truth.

questions.prompt: Mira is revising a risk memo full of words like likely and serious possibility. What move best fits the chapter?
choices: Leave the language alone so the team stays flexible
Replace the phrases with percentages, dates, and conditions
Remove the forecast section entirely until certainty is available

explanation.gentle: The chapter wants the memo turned into a claim the team can later compare with what happened.
explanation.direct: Choice B converts verbal blur into measurable accountability.
explanation.competitive: Pin the forecast down so it cannot slither away later.

questions.prompt: What is the main trap in always staying near 50 percent?
choices: It guarantees overconfidence
It can look prudent while avoiding useful distinctions
It makes Brier scoring impossible

explanation.gentle: Safe middle numbers can protect a forecaster from embarrassment while also keeping them from saying anything sharp enough to help.
explanation.direct: The chapter warns that low resolution can disguise itself as modesty.
explanation.competitive: Camping in the middle can be cowardice wearing caution.

questions.prompt: Why do foxes usually outperform hedgehogs once forecasts are scored?
choices: Foxes are always smarter in every domain
Foxes use many smaller clues and revise more freely
Hedgehogs refuse to use any data

explanation.gentle: Foxes handle contradiction and smaller pieces of evidence better, which helps once the record starts judging them.
explanation.direct: Measured forecasting rewards revisable thinking more than one-big-idea rigidity.
explanation.competitive: The scoreboard punishes theory loyalty when reality keeps pushing back.

questions.prompt: Lian keeps saying maybe the flight price will drop. What would improve her judgment most?
choices: Turning the hunch into a probability and a deadline
Avoiding all numbers because travel is unpredictable
Waiting until the decision disappears on its own

explanation.gentle: The chapter favors making the claim explicit enough to guide action and later learning.
explanation.direct: A probability plus time window is better than a verbal hedge that never becomes testable.
explanation.competitive: Maybe cannot be corrected. A number can.

questions.prompt: What does aggregation add that a lone forecaster often lacks?
choices: A guarantee that every estimate becomes more optimistic
Several partial views that can outperform one narrow angle
A way to avoid ever changing your mind

explanation.gentle: Aggregation matters because different people often see different useful parts of the same problem.
explanation.direct: The chapter treats combined disciplined judgments as a protection against individual blind spots.
explanation.competitive: Several clean fragments can beat one polished tunnel vision.

questions.prompt: Why does the chapter insist on keeping task difficulty attached to Brier scores?
choices: Because the same raw score can mean different things in easy and hard environments
Because Brier scores only work in political forecasting
Because difficult forecasts should never be quantified

explanation.gentle: A number looks cleaner than it is if the terrain behind it disappears from view.
explanation.direct: Context matters because identical scores can reflect very different levels of forecasting skill.
explanation.competitive: Do not let a neat metric flatter weak terrain.

questions.prompt: If Chapter 3 makes the record public, what question does that naturally set up next?
choices: Which forecasters keep outperforming once their judgments are scored
Whether forecasting should return to verbal language
Whether all grand theories are useless in every context

explanation.gentle: Once the scoreboard is real, the obvious next question is who actually keeps doing well under it.
explanation.direct: The chapter bridges naturally toward the people and processes that survive public measurement.
explanation.competitive: The next fight is not about whether to score. It is about who wins when scoring starts.
